detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.name: MISO
sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.name: Southwest Power Pool
sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The EIA commercial-sector sales snapshot for June 2026 totals 54,797.55 across the eight listed states, with Texas at 15,753.83, California at 10,024.68, and Virginia at 7,770.67. Because data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, these figures are a proxy for data center load, not a direct measurement. The average commercial price ranges from 8.66 in Texas to 27.33 in California, with Virginia at 10.99 and Ohio at 13.77, so Texas and Virginia show relatively low commercial electricity prices in this snapshot.

Across the five interconnection queues, the combined planned capacity waiting to connect is 1,326,605.64 MW. Storage accounts for 326,230.58 MW of that total when summing ERCOT, MISO, SPP, and CAISO, while gas accounts for 184,345.01 MW across all five queues. These queue totals are planned generation and storage waiting to connect, not data center demand itself, but the large storage and gas volumes track the load growth that data centers are adding. ERCOT alone lists 159,820.34 MW of storage and 78,092.4 MW of gas in its queue, the largest storage figure among the four queues that break out storage.

The sources are not directly comparable because each grid operator publishes its queue differently, and NYISO's queue is dominated by an "other" category of 291,156.45 MW that is not broken out further. CAISO's queue is much smaller at 71,608.82 MW, with storage at 46,870.26 MW and gas at only 915.6 MW, while MISO and SPP show more balanced mixes of solar, wind, storage, and gas. The EIA commercial sales snapshot covers only eight states and one month, so it cannot be directly matched to these queue regions. What to watch next is whether the storage and gas volumes in ERCOT, MISO, and SPP queues continue to rise in the next monthly reports, since that would signal more capacity being positioned for data center load.
